note: The desire to know. Dante opens his Convivio with Aristotle's saying that all people by nature desire to know. Here he is burning to learn why the mountain shook at the end of Canto 20.

In John 4, Jesus meets a woman of Samaria at a well and offers her "living water": whoever drinks it will never thirst again. She asks him for it. The water is the truth of God, the only thing that ends the mind's thirst.
The fifth terrace of Purgatory, where the souls of the greedy lie face down, bound to the ground they loved too much (Canto 19).

Luke 24: on the day of the Resurrection, two disciples walking to the village of Emmaus are joined by Christ and do not know him at first. The comparison fits: this soul has just risen too, set free from his penance.
The risen Christ's greeting to his disciples in the same chapter of Luke: "Peace be unto you."

context: The stranger is about to name him as the poet he loves most, without knowing he is speaking to him.

note: In Dante's Italian these three lines are Virgil's reply. He wishes the stranger peace in Heaven, and adds that the same court has sentenced him, Virgil, to eternal exile in Limbo. The stranger's surprised question follows.

context: Only saved souls climb here, so the stranger is startled to hear of anyone on these slopes who is shut out of Heaven.

note: At the gate of Purgatory an angel cut seven letter P's on Dante's forehead with a sword, for the seven deadly sins (peccata in Latin). One is wiped away as he leaves each terrace. Three are still there.

quote: she who spins day and night
note: Lachesis, one of the three Fates of Greek myth, who spins the thread of each life. Virgil means simply that Dante is still alive.
Another of the three Fates. In the version Dante follows, Clotho loads the wool onto the distaff, Lachesis spins it into thread, and Atropos cuts it at death.

quote: it doesn't see as we do
note: A living soul sees through the eyes of the body, and cannot find its own way through the world of the dead.

context: Hell is a funnel, and Limbo is its wide upper rim. Virgil was called from there to guide Dante (Inferno 2).

quote: as far as my knowledge can take him
note: Dante's word is "school". Virgil's teaching is human reason, which can lead Dante to the top of the mountain and no further. Beatrice takes over there.
At the end of Canto 20 the whole mountain shook, and every soul on it cried out "Glory to God in the highest", the song of the angels at Christ's birth.
Dante says its "wet feet": the shore at the bottom of the mountain, washed by the sea.
Above its gate, Purgatory has no weather. Nothing made of earth, air or water disturbs it. Whatever happens there is caused by Heaven alone, and here that means a soul going up to Heaven.
The three steps at the gate of Purgatory proper (Canto 9). Below them lies Ante-Purgatory, where souls wait and where rain and wind still reach.
Dante calls it "the daughter of Thaumas": Iris, goddess of the rainbow and messenger of the gods in classical myth.

Medieval science, following Aristotle, explained weather by two kinds of vapor rising from the earth. Moist vapor made rain, snow and dew. Dry vapor made wind, and when trapped underground it made earthquakes.
The angel who guards the gate, holding the two keys of Saint Peter (Canto 9).
Every soul on the mountain rejoices when one of them is set free. Nobody envies him: his release is good news for all.
No angel announces that a penance is finished, and no term is fixed. The soul simply finds one day that it wants to rise, and that wanting is the proof it is clean.

A distinction found in Thomas Aquinas. The soul always wants Heaven in the end. But while it is still stained, a stronger wish holds it to its pain: it wants to make amends, as eagerly as it once wanted to sin. The souls here are not prisoners. They stay because they choose to.
On this one terrace. He died about 1,200 years before Dante's journey. Canto 22 accounts for more than four hundred of the other years, spent on the terrace of sloth.

context: Dante held that the destruction of Jerusalem was God's punishment for the Crucifixion, carried out through Rome. Paradiso 6 and 7 return to the idea.

note: The name of poet.
Not yet a Christian. No historical source says he ever became one. His conversion seems to be Dante's own invention, and Canto 22 tells the story.

A mistake Dante shared with his age, which confused the poet with a teacher of rhetoric from Toulouse who had the same name. The poet was born in Naples. He says so in a book of poems that was lost in the Middle Ages and found again a century after Dante's death.
A poet's crown. Laurel was the usual one. Myrtle was the plant of Venus, and why Dante chose it here is not agreed.

context: He has just finished more than five hundred years on this terrace, and the earthquake was for him. He will climb with Dante and Virgil to the top of the mountain.

quote: I sang of Thebes, then of great Achilles
note: His two epics. The Thebaid tells of the war between the two sons of Oedipus for the throne of Thebes. The Achilleid was to tell the whole life of Achilles.
He died with the Achilleid barely begun. It breaks off in its second book.
Virgil's epic of Aeneas and the founding of Rome. The real Statius ends his Thebaid by telling his poem not to rival "the divine Aeneid" but to follow it at a distance and worship its footsteps.
Dante's image is of a scale: without the Aeneid, "I would not have weighed a dram", a tiny unit of weight.
A startling thing for a saved soul to say at the moment of his release: he would put off Heaven for a year to have known Virgil. Dante says "one sun", one circuit of the sun.
One of the few comic moments in the poem. Dante knows who is standing beside him, Virgil signals him to say nothing, and his face gives the secret away.

quote: who guides my eyes toward heaven
note: The line carries a sad irony: Virgil leads Dante up toward a Heaven he will never see himself.
To clasp the feet or knees was a gesture of deep reverence, of a disciple before his master.

quote: you're a shade, and you see a shade
note: Shades have no bodies to hold: Dante's arms passed straight through his friend Casella in Canto 2. Yet in Cantos 6 and 7 the poet Sordello embraced Virgil. Readers have long noticed the difference. Virgil's refusal here also has modesty in it.
Dante's word is "vanity", emptiness. Statius's love made him forget, for a moment, that both of them are dead.
